utterances.text: Does that mean that you could use that road only if given such a permit signed by this person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, only under those conditions. I had to have such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher. We no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at some point an attempt, an attempted attack on Prijedor was carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of May at four or five in the morning, we could hear shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: No. We knew nothing, but the radio later reported that a group of Muslims, that is, a Muslim unit had entered the old part of town, the new hotel, and they used boats for this. I think that a Captain Karlica from -- he was some kind of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to please keep your answers as short as possible. This way we'll move on much faster. Could you hear any artillery fire or small arms fire?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. That I heard later, about eight or ten in the morning. It was a mixed artillery and small arms fire. My house is on high ground, so I could hear it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did a Muslim family come to you during that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes, sometime. Maybe it was around noon or maybe ten or eleven or sometime. This was all the way back in 1992. A group of seven Muslims and an ethnic Serb was also with them. They came to me. It was Asim Crnalic, a very well-known family in that part of town, the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did these people end up in front of your house on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: My house is set in from the road, about 20 metres. I saw this group. There was this Mr. Asim and his wife Esma, and they had two children, two sons, two daughters-in-law, two children, and I saw him crying. I called him in, and he said, "Please, you can kill me, but help these two children survive."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your house the first where they turned in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: No. Apparently they thought that somebody else would help them. They came to somebody else's door, but they turned them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who brought them there to your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: They told us that they were brought by Damir Dosen. I only knew him as Kajin. I knew where his house was, but I didn't know that his name was Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did these people stay in your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: This man, he was one of the son-in-laws. He was an ethnic Serb. He stayed there with his family about a month, and Asim with Ceric [as interpreted] and the son Damir, they spent about seven days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While they were staying in your house, did you learn how they ended up in your house? I mean, in what manner did they come?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Mr. Asim was wondering himself. Apparently he -- there was this chaos, the war was going on, and that Davor [as translated] Dosen, probably because of this young boy Damir, that is why he gave them a lift.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether Damir ever knew them from before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: I believe that they did not know him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Damir ever come to your house while the Crnalics were still there in your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. He brought coffee. In fact, that's what my wife told me, that he had brought some coffee, and he came to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did these people ask Damir Dosen to bring them to your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: At that time, these people of these ethnic groups were being collected and taken to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is, why did Crnalics end up in your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: The son-in-law of Crnalics was from my home village, and he even, I think, was helping my father as an assistant hair cutter, barber, and that's why he probably remembered me, and that's how he ended up in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The people who were your neighbours, did they exert any pressure because, after the attack on Prijedor, a Muslim family landed in your house?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. Mladjo Undala, one of my neighbours, saw this -- one of the -- the other son-in-law, who was an ethnic Muslim, and told others in the neighbourhood that I was keeping Muslims in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the next document, please, and tell us what it is and where -- how you came in the possession of this document. Will you please read it and tell us, then, how did you come by it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: I went to the headquarters of the local commune. I was under threat of an attack. My wife -- my son came to me and told me that the neighbours were saying how my house should be blown up. And because I had a wife who was an ethnic Croat and Muslims in the house, I went to the local commune headquarters, and Marinko Coric was in charge there. I asked him to give me a written guarantee of sorts because I felt responsible for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So did you request to be given this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. I requested it for the safety of the persons who were in my house, and I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the lower -- on the bottom of the document, is that something that you added?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to note who had brought them, and I said that it was Dosen the tall, because there were two brothers and this was the tall one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the police come looking for Crnalics?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SOVILJ
utterances.text: Yes. A vanload of police arrived, and I didn't know any one of them. They asked me whether there were any Muslims in my house. I told them that, yes, there were. I showed them this certificate proving that I had reported them with the local commune, that I was responsible for them, as it is stated here, and they went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, looking at the clock, shall I go on or shall we continue tomorrow morning to conclude the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Petrovic, we'll take the adjournment now. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may just raise an issue of some concern to the Prosecution. I thought we should do it now before waiting till tomorrow, and that has to do with the -- not only the adequacy of the summaries we've been provided with, but of the three witnesses provided today, we have had incorrect information which, in effect, does not assist us or prevents us from adequately preparing for cross-examination. For example, the very first witness by name, we had the wrong birth date provided to us. Of course, we do, we do checks on names. We do checks on birth dates, and if they don't match, we move on. Secondly, with respect to the Witness DL, of more serious consequence, in the witness list of the Defence that was filed, we were given a person by a name with a different given name than the one that actually showed up today. That's very significant to us with respect to our ability to prepare for cross-examination. A different individual comes forward than the one that we anticipate is coming forward. The third witness today -- well, for example, the first one we also had a wrong birth date. I think they said it was the 4th of August, and we got the witness taking the stand, saying it was the 4th of January. These are significant things. Even this particular witness, we weren't given an adequate birth date, we just had a month. We don't have a birth date, et cetera. Now hopefully -- and I'm not for a moment suggesting that my friends are doing this in order to put us off, don't get me wrong, but the effect of the inattention to detail on matters of this nature, it does adversely affect our ability to perform our task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're talking about the outlines?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, the Defence witness list which was filed under 65 ter. For example, number 6 that was listed there, who has since received the pseudonym of DL, was listed by a different first name than the individual who in fact testified today. In other words, they're different people. So when we do our checks and prepare for cross-examination, we're prepared to cross-examine Mr. X, and instead we get Mr. Y. That is a problem. The second thing is about the adequacy of these lists. The Court has ordered summaries. We provided thorough summaries. It's a matter of degree as to what assists the Court, but with the greatest of respect, the summaries that we've been getting -- for example, in some of these instances we have no idea, for example, that the witness is going to testify about having been acquainted with one of the accused in these proceedings. That is for the Court to decide in terms of how adequate these are. What I don't want them to be is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, there are two matters. The witness list is produced pursuant to Rule 65 ter, and that's an obligation. I think you have a duty to ensure that it is as accurate as possible. With regard to the witness outline, that's a wholly administrative procedure devised by the Chamber, but if it is to assist the Court, then that, too, has to be accurate, and perhaps you would want to look at the other outlines that you are going to prepare and ensure that perhaps there could be a little more detail put, and also attend to the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, just very briefly in response to the mistake in the summary, it is one letter in the first name. It is a J instead of N. They are both legitimate first names. So I apologise for that. We are trying to do our best. But also, let me tell you that there are things that come up in the examination that we ourselves had not anticipated. But I will do my best to be as accurate as possible so that we don't bring about a situation where anybody would be misled, the Trial Chamber or my learned friends. And I also invited my learned friend, if there is any point which is vague or not clear enough, I would invite him to address me rather than bring it out to you. That is, first try to get any clarification from me. But I hope that we will be able to avoid all future misleading -- misunderstandings in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree with my friend that I would of course prefer to raise it with my learned friends. They have been very cooperative in dealing with the Prosecution. The trouble is the summaries we received this morning, so we didn't have a chance, and it wasn't until the witness actually took the stand that we understood it was a different name. But there is another issue; I may as well raise it now. We have just received a revised Defence witness list, and under number 2, like Roman numeral II, number 3, there is a name on there which was not included in the original witness list, and therefore is not -- there is not a 65 ter -- just a new name altogether, just appeared out of nowhere. I just want to raise that issue. And we as of yet have no summaries for tomorrow's witnesses. And I don't know, do we have two videolink witnesses tomorrow, plus others? Maybe we could clarify that so that we can start preparing this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First off, the practice of the Prosecution was to provide summaries at the time when the witnesses were practically coming out to give evidence, and in that respect I see no difference between the approach of the Dosen Defence and the OTP procedures. And as far as the videolink is concerned, I think it's perfectly clear, and we can clear it up without taking any time to the Trial Chamber. We have been diligent, I believe, because we have made an attempt - and I think we've succeeded - in paring down the list of 20, 21 witnesses, in compliance with what the idea was behind the Trial Chamber's urging us to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apart from the two videolink witnesses, do you have others in the event that those are concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. It was already last week that I told my learned friends, that I notified them that we had seven witnesses in The Hague, and in case of any problem with the videolink, that we can call them in so that we -- the Chamber doesn't have to waste time waiting for the link. We have seven witnesses here who are ready to jump in whenever there is a break in the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic, and you will provide the Prosecution and other Defence counsel with outlines as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Sir Ivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This might be an appropriate moment, since we are dealing with these matters, to raise a completely different one. Might I respectfully ask the Court when we can expect to receive the written reasons for the bis 98 ruling of the court? Its relevance to the Defence is perhaps obvious, as far as Kolundzija is concerned. There is difficulty about calling some witnesses, who are understandably reluctant to come, and depending upon the reasons that the Court has given, it may not be necessary to call some witnesses. On the other hand, it may be necessary to call others that we are not sure were so necessary. So it would be very helpful. I say this not to put pressure upon the Court. I don't know what the normal procedure is as to the time of producing the written reasons, but it would be helpful if we could know those written reasons before we started finalising the preparation of the defence of Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Subject to translation, it will be ready next week. Mr. Sovilj, we are going to take the adjournment for the afternoon, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.30. During the adjournment, I remind you you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes the members of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
